claim: C. elegans males live significantly shorter when maintained in groups, whereas the longevity of hermaphrodites is not influenced by population density.
source: Sex-specific longevity patterns also exist in Caenorhabditis elegans: males live significantly shorter when maintained in groups, whereas the longevity of hermaphrodites is not influenced by population density (Gems and Riddle, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gems and Riddle, 2000

claim: The lifespan of Caenorhabditis females is shortened after mating through receipt of male sperm and seminal fluid.
source: The lifespan of Caenorhabditis females is shortened after mating through receipt of male sperm and seminal fluid (Shi and Murphy, 2014), and separately by exposure to male pheromone (Maures et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shi and Murphy, 2014 and Maures et al., 2014

claim: Caenorhabditis females' lifespan is shortened by exposure to male pheromone.
source: The lifespan of Caenorhabditis females is shortened after mating through receipt of male sperm and seminal fluid (Shi and Murphy, 2014), and separately by exposure to male pheromone (Maures et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maures et al., 2014

claim: Just two C. elegans males together significantly reduced each individual's lifespan.
source: C. elegans male lifespan is very sensitive to male density: just two males together significantly reduced each individual's lifespan, and grouping eight males decreases lifespan by more than 35%, whereas the lifespan of C. elegans hermaphrodites is not affected by population density (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: Grouping eight C. elegans males decreases lifespan by more than 35%.
source: C. elegans male lifespan is very sensitive to male density: just two males together significantly reduced each individual's lifespan, and grouping eight males decreases lifespan by more than 35%, whereas the lifespan of C. elegans hermaphrodites is not affected by population density (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: The lifespan of C. elegans hermaphrodites is not affected by population density.
source: C. elegans male lifespan is very sensitive to male density: just two males together significantly reduced each individual's lifespan, and grouping eight males decreases lifespan by more than 35%, whereas the lifespan of C. elegans hermaphrodites is not affected by population density (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: Eight grouped daf-22(m130) males lived almost as long as solitary wild-type males.
source: Eight grouped daf-22(m130) males lived almost as long as solitary wild-type males, suggesting that male pheromone kills grouped wild-type males (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Male pheromone kills grouped wild-type males.
source: Eight grouped daf-22(m130) males lived almost as long as solitary wild-type males, suggesting that male pheromone kills grouped wild-type males (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that daf-22 males (pheromone-deficient) live as long as solitary wild-type males when grouped

claim: C. elegans males are more sensitive to male pheromone toxicity than hermaphrodites.
source: This low dosage of male pheromone had no effect on hermaphrodites, but significantly reduced C. elegans male lifespan (Figure 1D,E), suggesting that males are more sensitive than hermaphrodites to male pheromone toxicity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential effects on males vs hermaphrodites in Figure 1D,E

claim: Exposure to pheromone secreted by just one male was sufficient to significantly reduce the lifespan of C. elegans males.
source: In fact, we found that exposure to pheromone secreted by just one male was sufficient to significantly reduce the lifespan of C. elegans males (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Blocking male germline proliferation prevents male pheromone's effects on gene expression.
source: To our surprise, this comparison revealed no differences in gene expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), even at a high % False Discovery Rate (FDR), suggesting that blocking male germline proliferation prevents male pheromone's effects on gene expression.
evidence: Supported by microarray data showing no gene expression changes when FUdR is present, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: There was no lifespan difference when daf-22(m130) males were subjected to a high level of exogenous wild-type male pheromone in the presence of FUdR.
source: Indeed, we found that there was no lifespan difference when daf-22(m130) males were subjected to a high level of exogenous wild-type male pheromone (30 males per plate for conditioning) in the presence of FUdR, mimicking the microarray conditions (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G

claim: No population density-dependent lifespan decrease was observed when germline-deficient glp-1(e2141) males were grouped.
source: Furthermore, no population density-dependent lifespan decrease was observed when germline-deficient glp-1(e2141) males were grouped (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H

claim: Germline activity in the recipient is required for male pheromone-mediated death in both sexes.
source: Therefore, our results suggest that germline activity in the recipient is required for male pheromone-mediated death in both sexes.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing FUdR and glp-1 mutations prevent pheromone-mediated death

claim: The germline cannot be the site of pheromone production, but rather may modulate pheromone levels or quality.
source: However, males on plates conditioned by germline-less males still live shorter than the controls, suggesting that the germline cannot be the site of pheromone production, but rather may modulate pheromone levels or quality.
evidence: Inferred from observation that germline-less males still produce some pheromone effect, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F

claim: Solitary neuronally-masculinized hermaphrodites died earlier when exposed to a low level of male pheromone.
source: Solitary neuronally-masculinized hermaphrodites died earlier when exposed to a low level of male pheromone (eight males per plate for conditioning; Figure 2A), whereas normal hermaphrodites were insensitive to male pheromone at this concentration (Figure 1D), suggesting that sex-specific neuronal properties are responsible for male and hermaphrodite's different sensitivities to male pheromone's toxicity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Sex-specific neuronal properties are responsible for male and hermaphrodite's different sensitivities to male pheromone's toxicity.
source: Solitary neuronally-masculinized hermaphrodites died earlier when exposed to a low level of male pheromone (eight males per plate for conditioning; Figure 2A), whereas normal hermaphrodites were insensitive to male pheromone at this concentration (Figure 1D), suggesting that sex-specific neuronal properties are responsible for male and hermaphrodite's different sensitivities to male pheromone's toxicity.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that masculinizing neurons increases hermaphrodite sensitivity to male pheromone

claim: C. elegans males are normally attracted to pheromones secreted by old (self sperm-depleted) hermaphrodites.
source: C. elegans males are normally attracted to pheromones secreted by old (self sperm-depleted) hermaphrodites (Morsci et al., 2011; Leighton et al., 2014; Kleemann and Basolo, 2007), but males were not attracted to pheromones secreted by aged neuronally-masculinized hermaphrodites (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morsci et al., 2011; Leighton et al., 2014; Kleemann and Basolo, 2007

claim: Males were not attracted to pheromones secreted by aged neuronally-masculinized hermaphrodites.
source: C. elegans males are normally attracted to pheromones secreted by old (self sperm-depleted) hermaphrodites (Morsci et al., 2011; Leighton et al., 2014; Kleemann and Basolo, 2007), but males were not attracted to pheromones secreted by aged neuronally-masculinized hermaphrodites (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: When masculinized hermaphrodites were grouped, they lived shorter than the solitary controls.
source: More surprisingly, when these masculinized hermaphrodites were grouped, they lived shorter than the solitary controls (Figure 2C), suggesting that neuronal masculinization of the hermaphrodites is sufficient to induce the production of male-like pheromone in these hermaphrodites, and that neurons are key for male pheromone-mediated death.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Neuronal masculinization of the hermaphrodites is sufficient to induce the production of male-like pheromone in these hermaphrodites.
source: More surprisingly, when these masculinized hermaphrodites were grouped, they lived shorter than the solitary controls (Figure 2C), suggesting that neuronal masculinization of the hermaphrodites is sufficient to induce the production of male-like pheromone in these hermaphrodites, and that neurons are key for male pheromone-mediated death.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that grouped masculinized hermaphrodites die early like males

claim: Neurons are key for male pheromone-mediated death.
source: More surprisingly, when these masculinized hermaphrodites were grouped, they lived shorter than the solitary controls (Figure 2C), suggesting that neuronal masculinization of the hermaphrodites is sufficient to induce the production of male-like pheromone in these hermaphrodites, and that neurons are key for male pheromone-mediated death.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing neuronal masculinization affects both pheromone production and sensitivity

claim: Inhibiting germline proliferation in grouped masculinized hermaphrodites by FUdR rescued lifespan.
source: Inhibiting germline proliferation in these grouped masculinized hermaphrodites by FUdR rescued lifespan (Figure 2D), which again supports the conclusion that the germline, whether male or female, is required for male pheromone-mediated killing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The germline, whether male or female, is required for male pheromone-mediated killing.
source: Inhibiting germline proliferation in these grouped masculinized hermaphrodites by FUdR rescued lifespan (Figure 2D), which again supports the conclusion that the germline, whether male or female, is required for male pheromone-mediated killing.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing FUdR rescues lifespan in both males and masculinized hermaphrodites

claim: Mating decreased male lifespan ~35% compared with unmated solitary males.
source: Mating decreased male lifespan ~35% compared with unmated solitary males (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1), similar to the decrease in hermaphrodite lifespan caused by mating (Shi and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1

claim: Males die faster when paired with a hermaphrodite for a longer period.
source: Males die faster when paired with a hermaphrodite for a longer period: mating with a hermaphrodite for one day did not significantly affect the lifespan of the male, while 2–3 days' mating shortened male lifespan by 15%, 4–5 days' mating reduced their lifespan by 25%, and mating for 6 days reduced lifespan more than 35% (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The number of hermaphrodites paired with the single male during mating had little effect on male lifespan.
source: By contrast, the number of hermaphrodites paired with the single male during mating had little effect (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The time at which mating occurs within the reproductive period is not critical for males' post-mating lifespan decrease.
source: The time at which mating occurs within the reproductive period is also not critical for males' post-mating lifespan decrease; given the same mating duration, males mated with hermaphrodites for the first three days of adulthood had a similar lifespan decrease as those mated with hermaphrodites during days 6–8 of adulthood (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Males shrank after 6 days of mating; by Day 7, the mated males were 10% smaller than the unmated solitary males control.
source: As we previously observed in hermaphrodites (Shi and Murphy, 2014), males shrank after 6 days of mating; by Day 7, the mated males were 10% smaller than the unmated solitary males control (Figure 3E,F, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E,F and Supplementary file 2

claim: Male pheromone does not induce body shrinking.
source: No such shrinking was apparent when males were treated with male pheromone (Figure 3G), suggesting that mating and male pheromone act through different pathways.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Mating and male pheromone act through different pathways.
source: No such shrinking was apparent when males were treated with male pheromone (Figure 3G), suggesting that mating and male pheromone act through different pathways.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mating causes shrinking but pheromone does not

claim: Wild-type males still died early post-mating when paired with a daf-22 hermaphrodite for 6 days.
source: We wondered whether pheromone is required for mating-induced death in males; however, wild-type males still died early post-mating when paired with a daf-22 hermaphrodite for 6 days (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: daf-22 mutant males lived shorter after 6 days' mating with fog-2 hermaphrodites.
source: Likewise, daf-22 mutant males lived shorter after 6 days' mating with fog-2 hermaphrodites (Figure 4B), indicating that the post-mating lifespan decrease in our single-worm pair lifespan assay is due to mating itself rather than to the presence of pheromone from either sex.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The post-mating lifespan decrease in single-worm pair lifespan assay is due to mating itself rather than to the presence of pheromone from either sex.
source: Likewise, daf-22 mutant males lived shorter after 6 days' mating with fog-2 hermaphrodites (Figure 4B), indicating that the post-mating lifespan decrease in our single-worm pair lifespan assay is due to mating itself rather than to the presence of pheromone from either sex.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing mating effects persist in pheromone-deficient mutants

claim: When treated with 50 µM FUdR during the three-day mating period, males no longer died earlier.
source: This killing mechanism appears to be conserved in males: when treated with 50 µM FUdR during the three-day mating period, males no longer died earlier (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Germline-less glp-1(e2141) males experienced neither shrinking nor lifespan decrease after mating.
source: The absence of the germline also prevented mating-induced shrinking: germline-less glp-1(e2141) males experienced neither shrinking nor lifespan decrease after mating (Figure 4D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: Germline-mediated post-mating death and shrinking is conserved between C. elegans sexes.
source: These results suggest that germline-mediated post-mating death and shrinking is conserved between C. elegans sexes.
evidence: Inferred from observations in both males and hermaphrodites showing similar germline-dependent effects

claim: Only 14 genes were significantly up-regulated and 41 were significantly down-regulated in mated males compared to unmated males.
source: Only 14 genes were significantly up-regulated and 41 were significantly down-regulated (FDR = 0%; Figure 4F; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 4F and Supplementary file 3

claim: Mating decreases fat storage in males.
source: As we previously found in hermaphrodites (Shi and Murphy, 2014), mating decreases fat storage in males (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Vitellogenins were the top up-regulated genes in mated males, expressed on average 19 times higher in mated males than in solitary unmated males.
source: Surprisingly, vitellogenins (vit-4, vit-3, vit-5, vit-6, vit-2), which encode yolk protein precursors made in the female/hermaphrodite intestine for transport into developing oocytes (Kimble and Sharrock, 1983) and as such are not normally expressed in males (Figure 4G, left), were the top up-regulated genes in mated males, expressed on average 19 times higher in mated males than in solitary unmated males (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by microarray data in Supplementary file 3 and Figure 4G

claim: Vitellogenins are not normally expressed in males.
source: Surprisingly, vitellogenins (vit-4, vit-3, vit-5, vit-6, vit-2), which encode yolk protein precursors made in the female/hermaphrodite intestine for transport into developing oocytes (Kimble and Sharrock, 1983) and as such are not normally expressed in males (Figure 4G, left), were the top up-regulated genes in mated males, expressed on average 19 times higher in mated males than in solitary unmated males (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and established knowledge from Kimble and Sharrock, 1983

claim: Mating induced ectopic expression of VIT-2::GFP in the anterior intestine of males.
source: Mating induced ectopic expression of VIT-2::GFP in the anterior intestine of males, confirming our gene expression data.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G

claim: VIT-2::GFP expression induction in mated males was germline function-dependent.
source: Such expression induction was germline function-dependent, as FUdR treatment of males blocked VIT-2::GFP expression in mated males (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D

claim: Knocking down unc-62 was sufficient to rescue the lifespan decrease in mated males.
source: Using RNAi, we found that knocking down unc-62 was sufficient to rescue the lifespan decrease in mated males (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H

claim: The mis-expression of vitellogenins upon mating contributes to post-mating death in males.
source: Thus, the mis-expression of vitellogenins upon mating contributes to post-mating death in males.
evidence: Inferred from unc-62 RNAi rescue experiments and vitellogenin expression data

claim: Mated pqm-1(ok485) deletion males lived as long as unmated controls.
source: We found that mated pqm-1(ok485) deletion males lived as long as unmated controls (Figure 4I), suggesting that PQM-1 is also required for post-mating male death.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I

claim: PQM-1 is required for post-mating male death.
source: We found that mated pqm-1(ok485) deletion males lived as long as unmated controls (Figure 4I), suggesting that PQM-1 is also required for post-mating male death.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pqm-1 mutants do not die early after mating

claim: The pattern of gene expression in male pheromone-treated animals was very different from that of mated males.
source: Notably, this pattern of gene expression was very different from that of mated males (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Pearson correlation = −0.0594 for the whole transcriptome).
evidence: Supported by microarray comparison data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Upregulation of vitellogenin genes was not a signature of male pheromone-treated animals.
source: Specifically, upregulation of vitellogenin genes was not a signature of male pheromone-treated animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), also supporting the notion that the two pathways act through distinct molecular mechanisms.
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: MCP treatment caused no significant changes in fat metabolism gene expression.
source: While fat is reduced in males after mating (Figure 5B), MCP treatment caused no significant changes in fat metabolism gene expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) or Oil Red O staining (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by microarray and Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5C

claim: Mated wild-type worms lost about 30% of their glycogen stores post-mating in a germline-dependent manner.
source: Likewise, we found that mated wild-type worms lost about 30% of their glycogen stores post-mating in a germline-dependent manner (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: The mating-induced glycogen storage decrease and subsequent shrinking is conserved between sexes.
source: The mating-induced glycogen storage decrease and subsequent shrinking is conserved between sexes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), while glycogen stores are not affected by male pheromone (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5E

claim: Glycogen stores are not affected by male pheromone.
source: The mating-induced glycogen storage decrease and subsequent shrinking is conserved between sexes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), while glycogen stores are not affected by male pheromone (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: pqm-1(ok485) null mutant males were not short-lived when treated with male pheromone.
source: We found that pqm-1(ok485) null mutant males were not short-lived when treated with male pheromone (eight males per plate for conditioning; Figure 5F), suggesting that male pheromone killing, like mating-induced death, is mediated at least in part by PQM-1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F

claim: Male pheromone killing is mediated at least in part by PQM-1.
source: We found that pqm-1(ok485) null mutant males were not short-lived when treated with male pheromone (eight males per plate for conditioning; Figure 5F), suggesting that male pheromone killing, like mating-induced death, is mediated at least in part by PQM-1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pqm-1 mutants are resistant to male pheromone killing

claim: C. remanei males also lived significantly shorter after mating with a female C. remanei for 6 days.
source: We found that C. remanei males also lived significantly shorter after mating with a female C. remanei for 6 days (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: C. elegans males died early when mated with a C. remanei female for 6 days, even though no cross-progeny result from this mating.
source: While female death requires successful cross-progeny production (Shi and Murphy, 2014), C. elegans males died early when mated with a C. remanei female for 6 days (Figure 6B), even though no cross-progeny result from this mating.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The process of mating and up-regulation of male germline activity is sufficient to induce death, regardless of the species of the recipient female.
source: This result, together with the germline dependence of mating-induced death, suggests the process of mating and up-regulation of male germline activity is sufficient to induce death, regardless of the species of the recipient female.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that C. elegans males die after mating with C. remanei females despite no progeny production

claim: Neither C. remanei males nor females were short-lived when exposed to low levels of C. remanei male pheromone.
source: When exposed to low levels of C. remanei male pheromone (eight males per plate for conditioning), neither C. remanei males nor females were short-lived (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C,D

claim: At a higher concentration of male pheromone, multiple trials of C. remanei females and males on male-conditioned plates failed to reveal any sensitivity to either C. remanei or C. elegans male pheromone.
source: At a higher concentration (30 males per plate for conditioning), multiple trials of C. remanei females and males on male-conditioned plates failed to reveal any sensitivity to either C. remanei or C. elegans male pheromone (Figure 6E,F), in contrast to previous reports in which males and females were grouped (Maures et al., 2014); this result suggests that the lifespan shortening in the latter study was caused by mating rather than by male pheromone.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E,F

claim: C. elegans hermaphrodites died early when exposed to C. remanei male pheromone.
source: Interestingly, we found that male pheromone toxicity can act across species: C. elegans hermaphrodites died early when exposed to C. remanei male pheromone (Figure 6G), suggesting that the difference in sensitivity to male pheromone might stem from the perception of pheromone as a toxin, rather than from toxicity of the pheromone itself.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G

claim: The difference in sensitivity to male pheromone might stem from the perception of pheromone as a toxin, rather than from toxicity of the pheromone itself.
source: Interestingly, we found that male pheromone toxicity can act across species: C. elegans hermaphrodites died early when exposed to C. remanei male pheromone (Figure 6G), suggesting that the difference in sensitivity to male pheromone might stem from the perception of pheromone as a toxin, rather than from toxicity of the pheromone itself.
evidence: Inferred from cross-species pheromone experiments showing C. elegans are sensitive to C. remanei pheromone but C. remanei are not

claim: C. brenneri males are immune to male pheromone killing.
source: Like C. remanei males, two other gonochoristic species, C. brenneri and C. nigoni, are also immune to male pheromone killing (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: C. nigoni males are immune to male pheromone killing.
source: Like C. remanei males, two other gonochoristic species, C. brenneri and C. nigoni, are also immune to male pheromone killing (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: Males from C. briggsae died significantly earlier when exposed to male pheromone.
source: By contrast, males from two evolutionarily distant androdioecious species, C. briggsae and C. tropicalis, died significantly earlier when exposed to male pheromone (Figure 7C,D), just as C. elegans males do.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Males from C. tropicalis died significantly earlier when exposed to male pheromone.
source: By contrast, males from two evolutionarily distant androdioecious species, C. briggsae and C. tropicalis, died significantly earlier when exposed to male pheromone (Figure 7C,D), just as C. elegans males do.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Male pheromone-dependent killing is shared by males of androdioecious species.
source: These results strongly indicate that male pheromone-dependent killing is shared by males of androdioecious species.
evidence: Inferred from observations across three androdioecious species (C. elegans, C. briggsae, C. tropicalis) showing male pheromone killing

claim: Male pheromone significantly decreased male fertility.
source: Moreover, male pheromone significantly decreased male fertility (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B

claim: Male pheromone treatment decreases the number of progeny produced by those animals who do successfully mate.
source: Finally, male pheromone treatment decreases the number of progeny produced by those animals who do successfully mate (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C

claim: Male pheromone treatment did not affect the brood size of self-fertilized hermaphrodites.
source: By contrast, male pheromone treatment did not affect the brood size of self-fertilized hermaphrodites (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D

claim: Exposure to male pheromone during early life specifically reduces male fertility.
source: These results suggest that exposure to male pheromone during early life specifically reduces male fertility.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing male pheromone affects male fertility but not hermaphrodite brood size

claim: Male pheromone alone could effectively drive the population back to a primarily hermaphroditic state after several generations.
source: Male pheromone alone could effectively drive the population back to a primarily hermaphroditic state after several generations (Figure 8E).
evidence: Based on theoretical modeling shown in Figure 8E

claim: Germline-dependent early death after mating is conserved between sexes and perhaps even across great evolutionarily distances.
source: In summary, germline-dependent early death after mating is conserved between sexes and perhaps even across great evolutionarily distances, and is likely due to an unavoidable cost of mating, the result of mated animals ramping up germline proliferation and subsequently exhausting their own resources as quickly as possible to produce the next generation of progeny.
evidence: Inferred from observations across multiple species and both sexes showing similar germline-dependent mating effects

claim: Mated animals ramp up germline proliferation and subsequently exhaust their own resources as quickly as possible to produce the next generation of progeny.
source: In summary, germline-dependent early death after mating is conserved between sexes and perhaps even across great evolutionarily distances, and is likely due to an unavoidable cost of mating, the result of mated animals ramping up germline proliferation and subsequently exhausting their own resources as quickly as possible to produce the next generation of progeny.
evidence: Inferred from observations of germline-dependent resource depletion (glycogen, fat) and death after mating

claim: Androdioecious and gonochoristic species adopt different strategies to compete, mate, and maintain optimal sex ratios.
source: The differential use of pheromones as toxins or chemical messengers by males in androdioecious and gonochoristic species, respectively, demonstrates that they adopt different strategies to compete, mate, and maintain optimal sex ratios.
evidence: Inferred from comparative studies showing different pheromone effects in androdioecious vs gonochoristic species

claim: Women live longer than men in almost every country.
source: For example, women live longer than men in almost every country (WHO, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2016

claim: Interventions in longevity display sex-specific patterns in mice.
source: Moreover, interventions in longevity also display sex-specific patterns in mice (Austad and Fischer, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Austad and Fischer, 2016

claim: Males are usually very rare (less than 0.2% for the standard lab strain N2) in androdioecious species such as C. elegans.
source: In androdioecious species such as C. elegans, the population is dominated by hermaphrodites, which reproduce by self-fertilization. Males are usually very rare (less than 0.2% for the standard lab strain N2) and are produced through spontaneous X chromosome nondisjunction (Chasnov and Chow, 2002; Hodgkin, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chasnov and Chow, 2002; Hodgkin, 1983

claim: Under stressful conditions, more oocytes undergo chromosome non-disjunction in androdioecious species.
source: Under stressful conditions, more oocytes undergo chromosome non-disjunction; thus androdioecious species may periodically experience male population explosions (Chasnov and Chow, 2002; Hodgkin, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chasnov and Chow, 2002; Hodgkin, 1983

claim: The existence of males in androdioecious species reduces inbreeding and facilitates adaptation to changing environments.
source: The existence of males in androdioecious species reduces inbreeding and facilitates adaptation to changing environments (Anderson et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2010

claim: Neurons and the germline are required for male pheromone-dependent male death.
source: We find that neurons and the germline are required for male pheromone-dependent male death.
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing neuronal masculinization and germline requirements

claim: Hermaphrodites with a masculinized nervous system secrete male pheromone and are susceptible to male pheromone killing.
source: Hermaphrodites with a masculinized nervous system secrete male pheromone and are susceptible to male pheromone killing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Male pheromone-mediated killing is unique to androdioecious Caenorhabditis.
source: Male pheromone-mediated killing is unique to androdioecious Caenorhabditis, and may reduce the number of males in hermaphroditic populations; neither males nor females of gonochoristic species are susceptible to male pheromone killing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing androdioecious and gonochoristic species shown in Figures 6 and 7

claim: Male pheromone-dependent male death in C. elegans is due to the perception of male pheromone as a toxin.
source: Here we have found that male-specific population density-dependent death in C. elegans is due to the perception of male pheromone as a toxin; that is, while male pheromone itself is not a general poison to all worms, its perception by C. elegans males leads to death and to male-specific reproductive decline.
evidence: Inferred from cross-species experiments showing differential sensitivity to pheromone
